title: 'Not Satisfied': Trump Keeps Pressure on Iran as Deal Remains Elusive
summary: President Donald Trump made it clear on Wednesday: the United States is 'not satisfied' with the current state of negotiations with Iran, and time may be running out. Speaking at a cabinet meeting, Trump said Tehran is 'very much intent' on reaching an agreement to end the months-long conflict, but added a stark warning: 'So far, they haven't gotten there and we're not satisfied with it. But now we will be either that or will have to just finish the job.' The blunt language came just hours after Iranian state television broadcast what it claimed were details of a draft deal. The reported terms included the U.S. lifting its naval blockade of Iranian ports and, in return, Iran restoring commercial traffic through the strategic Strait of Hormuz to pre-war levels within a month. The strait, a narrow waterway through which about a fifth of the world's oil passes, has been effectively closed by Iran since the conflict erupted, sending global oil prices soaring. The White House swiftly dismissed the Iranian report as a 'complete fabrication.' Neither Trump nor Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who said there had been 'some progress and some interest' in talks, offered specifics on the remaining sticking points. Notably, the Iranian draft made no mention of Iran abandoning its nuclear ambitions or surrendering its stockpile of highly enriched uranium — issues central to U.S. demands. The conflict began on February 28 when the U.S. and Israel launched extensive strikes against Iran. Iran retaliated by attacking Israel and U.S.-allied Gulf states and mining the Strait of Hormuz. A ceasefire was agreed on April 8 and has largely held, but negotiations stalled in recent weeks. On Monday and Tuesday, the U.S. conducted what it called 'self-defense strikes' against Iranian missile sites and boats allegedly laying mines in southern Iran. Tehran denounced the strikes as a 'gross violation' of the ceasefire. Trump's comments underscore the fragile state of diplomacy. 'They're negotiating on fumes,' he said, suggesting Iran's position is weakening. Yet the path to a lasting agreement remains dangerously uncertain, with both sides seemingly far apart on core issues.
why_it_matters: The outcome affects global oil prices, which directly impact fuel costs and the price of goods you and your family use every day. A wider war could also draw in more countries and reshape the Middle East, influencing international relations for decades.

A narrow strip of water connecting two larger bodies of water; the Strait of Hormuz is a very important one for global oil shipping.
A form of uranium that has been processed to contain more of the type needed for nuclear reactors or, at very high levels, nuclear weapons.
Something that has been completely made up or invented, not based on truth.
Difficult issues in a negotiation that both sides cannot easily agree on and that block progress.
In this context, placing explosive devices in the water to damage or destroy ships.

background_read: The Strait of Hormuz, mentioned in the article, is a narrow waterway between Oman and Iran that connects the Persian Gulf to the Arabian Sea and the Indian Ocean. About 20% of the world's oil supply passes through it, making it one of the most important chokepoints in global energy markets. If the strait is blocked, oil prices can spike worldwide, affecting the cost of petrol and goods for everyday people.

President Donald Trump (who returned to the White House for a second, non-consecutive term in January 2025) has had a history of tense relations with Iran. In his first term (2017-2021), he withdrew the United States from the 2015 nuclear deal (the JCPOA), which had lifted some sanctions on Iran in exchange for limits on its nuclear program. Since then, U.S.-Iran relations have been marked by threats, proxy attacks, and periods of military confrontation.

The conflict described here began on February 28 after months of escalating tensions. Secretary of State Marco Rubio (a former senator from Florida, appointed by Trump in 2025) has been involved in diplomatic talks, but the fundamental question—whether Iran will give up its nuclear ambitions—remains a major obstacle. Ceasefires have been fragile in past conflicts in the region, and violations like the ones reported here often restart fighting.

perspectives.description: Trump and his team see strong military and economic pressure as the only way to force Iran to give up its nuclear program. They argue that past diplomatic deals allowed Iran to continue enrichment, so a tougher line is necessary. From this view, the self-defense strikes protect maritime traffic and deter further mining.

perspectives.perspective: Iran's and critics' stance (negative on U.S. actions)
perspectives.description: Iran portrays the U.S. strikes as violations of the ceasefire and evidence that Washington is not serious about peace. Critics point out that issuing ultimatums and bombing suspected sites undermine trust and make a lasting deal harder to achieve. They argue that a return to the 2015 nuclear framework could be a starting point.

The Strait of Hormuz has been a flashpoint for decades. Since the 1979 Iranian Revolution, the U.S. and Iran have repeatedly clashed over control of the waterway and broader Middle Eastern influence. This pattern shows that military standoffs often pause with fragile ceasefires that break down if the underlying disputes—especially over nuclear enrichment—remain unresolved.

If the current deadlock continues, the conflict could either escalate into a full-scale war involving Israel and Gulf states or force both sides back to serious negotiations. Regional powers like Saudi Arabia and the UAE, which are targets of Iranian retaliation, may push for a broader arrangement that addresses not just nuclear issues but also ballistic missiles and proxy militias.
